blocks.text: A developer writes `if (authenticated && tokenValid)` and then, in the `else` branch, guards a log message with `if (!authenticated && !tokenValid)`. The message never appears when only one of the two conditions fails, and nobody notices for months. The bug is not in the code — it is in the negation. De Morgan's law would have caught it in ten seconds.

blocks.markdown:
## Propositions and connectives

A **proposition** is a statement with a definite truth value. "Nigeria has 36 states" is a proposition; "sort the array" is not, since it is a command rather than a claim.

Compound propositions are built with connectives:

| Connective | Symbol | Code | True when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Negation | $\lnot p$ | `!p` | $p$ is false |
| Conjunction | $p \wedge q$ | `p && q` | both are true |
| Disjunction | $p \vee q$ | `p \|\| q` | at least one is true (inclusive) |
| Exclusive or | $p \oplus q$ | `p != q` | exactly one is true |
| Implication | $p \to q$ | `!p \|\| q` | *not* ($p$ true and $q$ false) |
| Biconditional | $p \leftrightarrow q$ | `p == q` | both have the same value |

Disjunction is **inclusive**: $p \vee q$ is true when both hold. Everyday English often means exclusive or ("tea or coffee"), and the mismatch is a steady source of specification errors.

blocks.title: Implication
blocks.text: $p \to q$ asserts only that a true $p$ guarantees a true $q$. It is false on exactly one assignment — $p$ true, $q$ false — and *vacuously true* whenever $p$ is false. So "if $n < 0$ then the array is sorted" is a true statement about every non-negative $n$, which is why a loop body that never executes cannot violate its postcondition.

blocks.caption: The one false row of the implication column is the whole content of the connective — memorise its position and the rest follows.

blocks.markdown:
### Tautology, contradiction, satisfiability

A formula with $n$ distinct variables has $2^n$ assignments. It is a **tautology** if true under all of them, a **contradiction** if false under all, and **satisfiable** if true under at least one. Two formulae are **logically equivalent**, written $\varphi \equiv \psi$, when their truth tables agree — equivalently, when $\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi$ is a tautology.

The exponential row count is not a presentational inconvenience. Deciding satisfiability of a propositional formula is the **boolean satisfiability problem**, the first problem proved NP-complete, and no algorithm is known that avoids exponential worst-case behaviour. Modern SAT solvers nevertheless handle formulae with millions of variables on structured instances, which is why they now sit inside compilers, verification tools and package dependency resolvers.

### The equivalences worth knowing by heart

**De Morgan's laws** — the negation of a conjunction is a disjunction, and conversely:

$$\lnot(p \wedge q) \equiv \lnot p \vee \lnot q \qquad \lnot(p \vee q) \equiv \lnot p \wedge \lnot q$$

This is the rule the opening example broke. Negating a guard means negating each operand **and** flipping the connective.

**Implication as disjunction** — $p \to q \equiv \lnot p \vee q$. Both formulae are false only when $p$ is true and $q$ false. This identity eliminates implication entirely and is the first step in converting a formula to conjunctive normal form.

**Contrapositive** — $p \to q \equiv \lnot q \to \lnot p$. Negate *and* swap. Distinguish it carefully from the two non-equivalent variants:

- **Converse** $q \to p$ — swap only. Not equivalent.
- **Inverse** $\lnot p \to \lnot q$ — negate only. Not equivalent.

The contrapositive is a legitimate proof strategy; the converse and inverse are the two commonest fallacies in informal reasoning.

blocks.latex: p \to q \;\equiv\; \lnot p \vee q \;\equiv\; \lnot q \to \lnot p, \qquad \lnot (p \to q) \;\equiv\; p \wedge \lnot q
blocks.caption: Four ways of saying the same thing. The last is how you negate an implication — and note there is no arrow in the result.

blocks.title: Verifying De Morgan's law by exhaustive truth table
blocks.prompt: Prove that ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q by constructing the full truth table, and state the practical consequence for negating a compound guard.

steps.text: Enumerate the assignments. With two variables there are $2^2 = 4$ rows: (T,T), (T,F), (F,T), (F,F).
Compute the left-hand side, $\lnot(p \wedge q)$. The conjunction is T, F, F, F across the four rows, so its negation is **F, T, T, T**.

Compute the right-hand side, $\lnot p \vee \lnot q$. Row 1: $\text{F} \vee \text{F} = \text{F}$. Row 2: $\text{F} \vee \text{T} = \text{T}$. Row 3: $\text{T} \vee \text{F} = \text{T}$. Row 4: $\text{T} \vee \text{T} = \text{T}$. So **F, T, T, T**.
Compare. The two columns agree in all four rows, so the formulae are logically equivalent and the biconditional between them is a tautology.

Check the tempting wrong answer. $\lnot p \wedge \lnot q$ gives F, F, F, **T** — it agrees only in rows 1 and 4 and is false in the two rows where exactly one operand fails. That is precisely the case the opening example silently dropped.

Practical consequence: `!(authenticated && tokenValid)` must be written `!authenticated || !tokenValid`. When negating a guard, negate every operand *and* swap `&&` with `||`. For nested guards, apply the law from the outside inwards until no negation sits in front of a bracket.

blocks.answer: Both sides evaluate to F, T, T, T, so $\lnot(p \wedge q) \equiv \lnot p \vee \lnot q$; negating a conjunction requires flipping the connective, not only the operands.

blocks.markdown:
### Valid inference and its two famous fallacies

An argument is **valid** when the conclusion is true in every assignment where all premises are true. Validity is a property of the *form*, so an argument can be valid with false premises and invalid with true ones.

| Form | Premises | Conclusion | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Modus ponens | $p \to q$, $p$ | $q$ | **Valid** |
| Modus tollens | $p \to q$, $\lnot q$ | $\lnot p$ | **Valid** |
| Hypothetical syllogism | $p \to q$, $q \to r$ | $p \to r$ | **Valid** |
| Disjunctive syllogism | $p \vee q$, $\lnot p$ | $q$ | **Valid** |
| Affirming the consequent | $p \to q$, $q$ | $p$ | *Invalid* |
| Denying the antecedent | $p \to q$, $\lnot p$ | $\lnot q$ | *Invalid* |

Both fallacies come from the same misreading — treating $p \to q$ as though it were $p \leftrightarrow q$. "If the build is broken the tests fail; the tests failed; therefore the build is broken" affirms the consequent, and it is wrong because a flaky test also makes the tests fail. Debugging is largely applied modus tollens: predict a consequence of your hypothesis, observe that it does not hold, and eliminate the hypothesis.

blocks.title: Logic is the specification language of programs
blocks.text: A precondition, a postcondition and a loop invariant are all propositions. A type system is a proof system. A short-circuit `&&` is a conjunction whose right operand is evaluated lazily. When you simplify a boolean guard using De Morgan or the implication identity, you are performing a formally justified program transformation, not a stylistic tidy-up.

points: A proposition has a definite truth value; connectives build compound propositions from simpler ones.
Disjunction is inclusive, unlike much everyday use of "or", which usually means exclusive.
$p \to q$ is false on exactly one assignment, $p$ true with $q$ false, and is vacuously true whenever $p$ is false.
A formula with $n$ variables has $2^n$ assignments, which is why satisfiability checking is exponential in the worst case.
De Morgan: negating a conjunction yields a disjunction of negations, and vice versa — flip the connective as well as the operands.
$p \to q \equiv \lnot p \vee q$, and its negation is $p \wedge \lnot q$ with no arrow remaining.
The contrapositive $\lnot q \to \lnot p$ is equivalent to the original; the converse and inverse are not.
Modus ponens and modus tollens are valid; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are fallacies caused by reading an implication as a biconditional.
